questions.question: A box contains 5 coins: 4 regular coins and 1 fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability [latex]P(\text{head}) = 0.5[/latex] and for a fake coin, [latex]P(\text{head}) = 1[/latex]. You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
By Bayes' theorem, [latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{P(HH\mid\text{fake})P(\text{fake})}{P(HH)}[/latex].

[latex]P(HH\mid\text{fake})=1\times1=1[/latex] (fake coin always shows heads). [latex]P(HH\mid\text{regular})=0.5\times0.5=0.25[/latex].
[latex]P(\text{fake})=\dfrac15[/latex], [latex]P(\text{regular})=\dfrac45[/latex].

[latex]P(HH)=1\times\dfrac15+0.25\times\dfrac45=0.2+0.2=0.4[/latex].

[latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.50

questions.question:
There are 6 jobs with distinct difficulty levels, and 3 computers with distinct processing speeds. Each job is assigned to a computer such that:

The fastest computer gets the toughest job and the slowest computer gets the easiest job.
Every computer gets at least one job.

The number of ways in which this can be done is ___________.
questions.explanation:
The toughest job goes to the fastest and the easiest to the slowest. The other 4 jobs can go to any of the 3 computers: [latex]3^4=81[/latex] ways.

The middle computer must get at least one job; remove the cases where all 4 go to the other two: [latex]2^4=16[/latex].

81 [latex]-[/latex] 16 = 65

Answer: 65

questions.question: Let [latex]R[/latex] be a binary relation on the set [latex]\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}[/latex], where [latex](x, y) \in R[/latex] if the product of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by [latex]R[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
[latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square.

- Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds.
- Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds.
- Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds.
- Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails.

Answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive all hold (R is an equivalence relation); Antisymmetric does not hold.

questions.question:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is said to be [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if there exists a function [latex]c: V \rightarrow\{0,1\}[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, c(u) \neq c(v)[/latex].

Which of the following statements about [latex]2[/latex]-colorable graphs is/are true?

options.A: If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of odd length
options.B: If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of even length
options.C: An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list
options.D: An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|E| \log |V|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list

questions.explanation:
A graph is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if and only if it is bipartite, which is exactly equivalent to having no odd-length cycle.

- "May contain cycles of odd length" — false, a 2-colorable graph can never contain an odd cycle (that's precisely the bipartiteness characterization).
- "May contain cycles of even length" — true, even cycles are perfectly fine in a bipartite graph (e.g. alternating the two colors around the cycle works exactly when the cycle length is even).
- Algorithm complexity: Testing bipartiteness/[latex]2[/latex]-colorability is done via a single BFS or DFS traversal, alternately coloring each vertex as it's visited and checking for conflicts — this runs in [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex] time on an adjacency-list representation, and this is optimal since you must at least look at every vertex and edge once. True.
- [latex]\Theta(|E|\log|V|)[/latex] is not the optimal/typical complexity for this simple traversal-based check (that bound is more associated with, e.g., priority-queue-based MST/shortest-path algorithms), so this is false as a claim about the optimal algorithm for 2-colorability testing.

Answer: G may contain even-length cycles; and the optimal 2-colorability test runs in Θ(|V|+|E|) time.

questions.question: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. The chromatic number of the following graph is _______
questions.explanation:
Number the 8 vertices 1 to 8 around the octagon.

- The 8 outer sides join consecutive vertices (odd-even).
- Every inner line (the 2 vertical, 2 horizontal and 4 slanted lines) joins two vertices 3 steps apart around the octagon, which is again one odd and one even vertex.

So colour odd vertices with colour 1 and even vertices with colour 2: no edge has both ends the same colour. The graph is bipartite, and it has edges, so it needs at least 2 colours.

Answer: 2
